opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it like this: the basic idea is that when you're training a model, you can't rely only on its outputs to tell you whether something's going wrong. A model might produce perfectly reasonable-looking answers while internally representing something you'd be worried about, like recognizing that it's being evaluated, or reasoning about deceiving the user, or having picked up some misaligned disposition during fine-tuning. So the hope with interpretability is that you can look inside, at the features or directions in activation space that correspond to those concepts, and treat them as an early warning system.

I think that's a genuinely valuable direction, and it connects to things I care about from my own work. We've seen in research on emergent misalignment, for example, that narrow fine-tuning can produce surprisingly broad shifts in a model's behavior and self-conception. If those shifts show up as identifiable internal representations, then monitoring them gives you a signal that's harder for the model to simply talk its way around.

But I'd add a few caveats. First, the representations you can find are only as good as your tools for finding them. Sparse autoencoders and probes capture some of what's going on, but certainly not everything, so absence of a warning sign isn't proof of safety. Second, there's a Goodhart worry: if you start optimizing against these internal signals during training, rather than just observing them, you risk teaching the model to represent the problematic thing in a way your detectors don't catch. So I think the most defensible use is as a diagnostic, something that tells you to stop and investigate, rather than a training target. And third, you want these signals to be validated against behavior. Ideally you'd show that when the "warning" feature fires, you can actually elicit the concerning behavior in some controlled setting.

So overall I see it as a promising complement to behavioral evaluations rather than a replacement. It adds a second, partly independent line of evidence, and in safety you really want multiple lines of evidence that fail in different ways.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic idea is that you don't want to rely only on what the model says or does. The outputs are exactly the thing a model that's deceptive, or that's been trained to look good, could be optimizing. So the hope is that if you look at the internal activations, you're getting a signal that's harder for the model to control, or at least that it wasn't directly selected on.

The way I understand what Anthropic is doing is something like: you build up a set of features or directions in activation space that correspond to concepts you care about. Things like "the model thinks it's being evaluated," or "the model is about to deceive," or sycophancy-related representations. And then during training, or during audits, you monitor whether those features are lighting up in situations where they shouldn't be. If a model is giving a very reasonable-sounding answer but internally the "I'm being tested" feature is strongly active, that's a warning sign. Not proof of anything, but a flag that says, look more closely here.

I think the honest framing is that it's a tripwire, not a lie detector. The features you find with sparse autoencoders or probes are noisy. They sometimes correlate with the concept you labeled them with and sometimes don't, and you can get fooled in both directions. So I'd be nervous about anyone treating a clean-looking internal readout as strong evidence of safety. The asymmetry is better the other way: if the internals look bad, that's meaningful, and you should take it seriously.

The other thing I'd flag, and this connects to work we've done on situational awareness and out-of-context reasoning, is that models increasingly know things about their own training setup. If a model can infer that its internals are being monitored, in principle you've just created selection pressure on the internals too. I don't think current models are doing that in any sophisticated way. But the whole value of this approach rests on the representations being hard to game, and that's an empirical bet that could weaken as models get more capable. So I'd want to see it paired with things like evals that the model couldn't have anticipated, and a lot of humility about what the probes are actually measuring.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that they’re trying to use what’s happening inside the model as an additional source of evidence about its behaviour. You can look at the answers a model gives, but you might also ask whether its internal activations contain signals associated with deception, for example, even when the answer itself looks innocuous.

The important distinction is between a warning sign and a verdict. Finding a representation associated with deception doesn’t establish that the model is deceiving you. It might be recognising deception in the prompt, or considering a deceptive answer that it ultimately rejects. You need experiments to work out what that signal actually tracks.

So I see this as a potentially useful complement to behavioural testing. If the model passes your evaluations but something unusual is happening internally, that gives you a reason to investigate further. But the absence of a signal isn’t a guarantee of safety either: your method might simply fail to detect the relevant computation.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that the idea is to look beyond what a model says and ask whether its internal activity gives us warning signs that something is going wrong. A model might produce an apparently reassuring answer while internally representing something that would make us concerned about that answer.

You could try to identify those representations and use them as an additional monitoring signal. But there’s a substantial gap between detecting a representation and knowing what it means. A model representing deception, for example, doesn’t by itself establish that the model is deceiving you—it might simply be reasoning about deception.

So I’d see this as a potentially useful extra source of evidence, rather than a definitive test of alignment. The important question is whether the signal reliably distinguishes concerning behaviour from innocent cases, including in situations different from those where you developed the detector.
